description: We are a team of biologists passionate about coastal conservation and remote sensing. Combining our ecological expertise with satellite data, we developed a mangrove monitoring application to track ecosystem changes over time and support environmental decision-making.
summary: Mangroves are estuarine ecosystems that play an important ecological rol because of the environmental services they provide, including their ability to sequester and store carbon. In the Veracruz–Boca del Río area, mangroves are exposed to various anthropogenic pressures that have contributed to the loss of vegetation cover. Between 2000 and 2023, this ecosystem lost 71.4 hectares, while the number of vegetation patches increased from 49 to 119. This situation highlights the importance of assessing changes in vegetation cover and condition using remote sensing tools, such as the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), which helps identify variations in vegetation photosynthetic activity and cover. Its application can support mangrove monitoring and the identification of vulnerable areas, providing valuable information for ecosystem management and conservation.
details:
ManglAPP is a web-based application designed to monitor and assess the health of mangrove ecosystems in the Arroyo Moreno Protected Natural Area (ANP) and the Mandinga Lagoon System in Veracruz, Mexico. The project works by processing satellite images and remote sensing technology to analyze changes in mangrove vegetation between 2000 and 2026, allowing users to identify areas experiencing degradation, fragmentation, or potential environmental threats.

Figure 1. Application user interface. Left: Year 2000 view. Right: Current view.

How does it work?

The application uses the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), calculated from Landsat satellite imagery, to evaluate vegetation conditions over time. It processes satellite data through Google Earth Engine, using spatial, spectral, and cloud masking techniques to improve the quality and reliability of the analysis.

ManglAPP features an interactive, mobile-friendly interface with a split-screen visualization and a comparison slider. These features allow users to compare satellite images from different years and observe changes in mangrove coverage. Additionally, the application incorporates a traffic-light classification system that identifies vegetation conditions as healthy, damaged, or endangered, making the results easier to understand.

Benefits and intended impact

The main benefit of ManglAPP is that it makes satellite-based environmental monitoring more accessible to people who do not have specialized knowledge of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) or remote sensing.

The project aims to:

1. Identify areas where mangrove vegetation has deteriorated over time.

2. Detects changes in vegetation cover and fragmentation patterns.

3. Highlight vulnerable areas that may require conservation or restoration actions.

4. Provide accessible environmental information to support decision-making.

5. Encourage community participation and strengthen local environmental awareness.

ManglAPP seeks to support mangrove conservation by providing a practical tool for understanding ecosystem changes and helping communities, researchers, and local authorities make more informed environmental decisions.

Through this approach, ManglAPP combines technology, environmental science, and NASA public data to promote better understanding and conservation of mangrove ecosystems.

Tools, programming languages, hardware, and software

Programming language: JavaScript, used to develop the application's functionality, process data interactions, and create its interactive interface.

Software: Google Earth Engine Apps, used to build and publish the interactive web application.

Methodology: We built a split-screen interactive interface using the Google Earth Engine (GEE) Apps development framework. The platform enables a simultaneous comparison between the historical baseline from the year 2000 (left panel) and updated monitoring data from 2026 (right panel).

We programmed the application using exclusion algorithms based on spatial and spectral masking. This allows the system to automatically discard urban areas, open water bodies, croplands, and terrestrial grasslands, isolating specifically the spectral signature and the intertidal zone where mangroves are found.

Spectral thresholding: excludes pixels that do not match the infrared and moisture signature typical of mangroves (discarding open water, concrete paving, or bare soil); cloud/Shadow masking: uses the landsat pixel quality band (QA_PIXEL) to automatically exclude clouds and shadows that would otherwise distort the NDVI calculation.

Data sources: NASA Earthdata - Vegetation Index; NASA Landsat Mission Data Overview; NASA Earthdata - Global Mangrove Forests Distribution; NASA Earthdata - Greenness Trends of Mangrove Forests Across Mexico; USGS/NASA Landsat Collection 2 Surface Reflectance; Google Earth Engine Cloud Platform; CONABIO - Sistema de Monitoreo de los Manglares de México (SMMM).

Hardware: MacBook Air (MacOs Monterey 12.7.6 & MacOs Sequoia 15.7.7) used for programming, application development, data analysis, and presentation. Cellphone Huawei Y9s for testing.

Creativity and innovation of MaglAPP

The creative aspect of ManglAPP lies in combining satellite remote sensing, environmental analysis, and an accessible web interface into a single monitoring tool. Instead of presenting complex satellite data and technical vegetation indices, the application translates this information into intuitive visual comparisons and a simple traffic-light classification system.

An innovative feature of the application is the ability to generate a polygon that defines the specific area of ​​interest corresponding to mangrove vegetation. This is achieved by incorporating UTM (Universal Transverse Mercator) coordinates, which allows users to delineate and customize the geographic boundaries of the area they wish to monitor. This functionality enables users to focus on specific mangrove areas while excluding other types of vegetation that are not relevant to the study and monitoring of mangroves.

Its interactive design allows users to explore historical changes in mangrove ecosystems without requiring specialized software or advanced technical skills. The combination of long-term satellite observations, customizable geographic boundaries, and an accessible interface makes environmental information easier to analyze, interpret, and communicate.

What factors we considered?

Scientific reliability: Use Landsat imagery and the NDVI index as indicators of vegetation status, applying appropriate masking techniques to reduce interference caused by clouds.

Spatiotemporal comparison: Ensure that users can compare different time periods, specifically the changes that occurred between 2000 and 2026.

Accessibility: Design a simple interface that can be used by individuals with no prior experience in Geographic Information Systems (GIS) or remote sensing.

Environmental relevance: We focus on mangrove ecosystems due to their ecological importance and high vulnerability resulting from anthropogenic pressure.

Through this approach, ManglAPP combines technology, environmental science, and NASA public data to promote better understanding and conservation of mangrove ecosystems.
